intro.html: There are many ways to help something along. You can make it easier (facilitate) or faster (expedite). You can help it grow, as a gardener helps a plant (foster, nurture, cultivate). You can stand up for it (champion), put your name behind it (endorse), keep it going (sustain) or jolt people into acting for it (galvanize).
One word in this family helps the wrong side: to abet is to help or encourage someone in doing wrong, as in the old legal phrase “aid and abet.”

words.def: to make an action or process easier
words.ex: A ramp {facilitated} moving the piano into the house.
words.ctx: The new bridge will {facilitate} trade between the two towns; farmers who once spent a day driving around the lake will reach the market in an hour.
words.etym: From French faciliter, from Latin facilis, “easy.”

mn.text: Instead of dragging the heavy piano up the steps, the movers roll it up a ramp. The ramp {facilitates} the job: it makes it easier.

scene.alt: A big man easily pushes a piano up a ramp.

words.ctx: To {expedite} the repairs, the city hired a second crew and kept the work going through the night, and the road reopened two weeks early.
words.etym: From Latin expedire, “to free the feet” (as from a snare), and so to set free, make ready: ex (out) + pes, ped- (foot).

mn.text: Ped means foot. To get the package there today, the shop sends its fastest runner out the door. It {expedites} the delivery.

scene.alt: A delivery runner races down the street with a package.

words.def: to encourage the growth or development of
words.ex: The art club {fosters} young talent with free paint and lots of praise.
words.ctx: The coach hoped to {foster} a sense of teamwork, so she paired older and younger players and had them practice every drill together.
words.etym: From Old English fostrian, “to nourish, feed.”
words.note: A foster family raises a child who is not its own by birth; the verb keeps that sense of helping something grow.

mn.text: With paint, space and praise, the art teacher helps her students improve faster than they ever could alone. She {fosters} their talent.

scene.alt: An art teacher claps as a proud boy paints at an easel.

words.def: to care for and help grow
words.ex: Lila {nurtured} the tiny seedlings with water and sunshine.
words.ctx: A good teacher does more than correct mistakes; she {nurtures} a student’s curiosity, feeding every question with a book, a walk or a new experiment.
words.etym: From Old French norriture, “food, upbringing,” from Latin nutrire, “to nourish.”

mn.cue: NURSE-ture: nurse it till it grows
mn.text: Granny Mae nurses the baby bird with drops of water until it is strong enough to fly. She {nurtures} it.

scene.alt: A grandmother gently feeds a baby bird in its nest with a spoon.

words.def: to develop something by steady care and effort
words.ex: Rosa {cultivated} a love of poetry by reading one poem every night.
words.ctx: Over many years the shopkeeper {cultivated} loyal customers, remembering their names, their children’s birthdays and how they liked their coffee.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin cultivare, from Latin colere, “to till the soil, tend,” the same root as agriculture and culture.
words.note: First used of fields and crops; now also of skills, friendships and tastes.

mn.text: Year after year, Omar tills, plants and weeds his garden until it blooms. In the same way, you can {cultivate} a skill with steady care.

scene.alt: A proud gardener with a rake stands beside a row of flowers that grow bigger and bigger.

words.def: to fight for or speak up for a cause or person
words.ex: Ms. Ortiz {championed} the idea of a school garden for years.
words.ctx: Long before the trail was popular, a few hikers {championed} it, writing letters, clearing brush and leading free walks until the town agreed to protect it.
words.note: As a noun, a champion is a winner, or a person who fights for a cause.

mn.cue: a CHAMP who fights FOR a cause
mn.text: Tia speaks up for the shelter dogs at every town meeting until the town builds them a new home. She {champions} their cause.

labels.text: a CHAMP fights FOR a cause

scene.alt: A woman holds up a sign for the shelter dogs at a town meeting, with a happy dog beside her.

words.ex: Three local chefs {endorsed} the new cookbook.
words.ctx: The doctors’ group did not merely allow the new playground rules; it {endorsed} them in a public letter, urging every school in the state to adopt them.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin indorsare, “to write on the back”: in (on) + dorsum (back). You endorse a check by signing its back.

mn.cue: EN-DORSE: sign your name on the BACK
mn.text: The chef signs the back cover of Lin’s cookbook and writes, “I recommend it!” She {endorses} it.

scene.alt: A chef signs the back of a cookbook while its delighted author cheers.

words.def: to keep something going; to support it over time
words.ex: Hot soup {sustained} the hikers on the long, cold climb.
words.ctx: The little theater could not {sustain} itself on ticket sales alone, so neighbors held bake sales every month to keep its doors open.
words.etym: From Latin sustinere, “to hold up from below”: sub (under) + tenere (to hold).

mn.cue: SOUP-STAIN: the soup keeps them going
mn.text: Their jackets have soup stains, but the hot soup keeps the hikers going all the way up the mountain. Food that keeps you going {sustains} you.

scene.alt: Two hikers with backpacks enjoy steaming bowls of soup on a mountain trail.

words.def: to help or encourage someone, usually in doing wrong
words.ex: The guard who looked the other way {abetted} the smugglers.
words.ctx: Kai did not take the cookies himself, but he {abetted} his little brother by holding the ladder and keeping watch for Mom.
words.note: Usually in the phrase “aid and abet,” which means to help someone commit a crime.

mn.cue: A BET: “I bet no one sees!”
mn.text: “Go on, I bet no one sees!” Rex whispers, holding the ladder steady while Pip reaches for the cookie jar. Rex {abets} the mischief.

scene.alt: A sneaky teen whispers encouragement as a boy on a stool reaches for the cookie jar.

words.def: to shock or excite people into action
words.ex: The coach’s speech {galvanized} the tired team.
words.ctx: News that the old oak would be cut down {galvanized} the neighborhood; within a day, two hundred people had signed a petition and filled the town hall.
words.etym: Named for Luigi Galvani, an Italian scientist of the 1700s who made frog muscles twitch with electric current; the word first meant to stimulate with electricity.
words.note: Galvanize also means to coat iron with zinc to stop rust (a galvanized pail).

mn.cue: the GAL in the VAN jolts them awake
mn.text: The gal in the van blasts her horn, and the sleepy campers leap out of their tents, ready to go. She {galvanizes} them.

scene.alt: A woman with a megaphone wakes the campers, who leap up full of energy.

head: how it helps
words
after.cap: Ten ways to help, one of them shady.

after.html: Writers rarely use abet for good deeds. If a character abets someone, expect trouble: the getaway driver abets the robbers.

items.q: Which sentence uses abet the way careful writers do?
choices: The lookout abetted the thieves by whistling when the guard came.
The nurse abetted the patient’s recovery with good care.
The librarian abetted the children’s love of books.
The sunshine abetted the growth of the tomatoes.
items.why: Abet usually means helping someone do wrong. For good help, use foster, nurture or facilitate.

items.q: The speech galvanized the crowd. The crowd was…
items.why: To galvanize people is to jolt them into action. (Coating metal with zinc is a different, technical sense.)

items.q: Which word comes from Latin words meaning “to free the feet”?
items.why: Expedite: ex (out) + ped (foot). Freed feet move fast, so to expedite is to speed something up.

items.q: True or false: to endorse a plan is to publicly support it.
items.why: True. Endorse first meant to sign on the back of a document; now it means to approve publicly.
